$comment: THE STAGE TABLE — the one place a stage's status is recorded.
`scripts/docs.test.mjs` reads this file. Two rules make it more than a list:
1. A stage may not be `shipped` while any `DEFER(engine-N)` marker in the
tree names it. A stage table that has started lying is worse than none,
because it is re-read and believed by somebody with no memory.
2. Every guard's `stage` names a row here, so a guard cannot protect work
that is not on the map.
`ends` is the exit criterion — an observable, not a feeling. It is what makes
`shipped` a claim somebody could check rather than a decision somebody made.

stages.title: Ground — workspace, docs, guard registry, standards
Kernel — entities, declarations, gate algebra, problems
Directory + placement
Runtime — manifest → live worker
Identity + tenancy
Surface — HeroUI shell, nav, sky, rendered settings
Money — plans, entitlements, credits, jobs
Services — ai and notify over RPC
Vault + legal
A real product on OneEngine, end to end
One — the deployment and the OneSpace
The agent surface — every operation an MCP tool, derived
Multi-app access — a platform role for the workspace, a role per app inside it
The package rail — a priced bundle of timed grants, one ledger, one clock
The tenant centre — the shell with the router: five areas + app screens inside
The operator console — the same shell on `admin.`, and the maintenance switch
AI actions — a lane per action, a model the operator binds, words that narrow
OneSpace — one surface over the product, reachable from every door, addressed
OneDesign — the design system named, packaged, documented and fenced
Workspaces — personal or commercial, one brand, one installable, a shard of their own
Payment — a workspace subscribes, and only a signed event stamps the plan
OneSpace — `id`, `admin` and `setup` merge into one address off the workspace root
Mail that leaves the process — a letter, its variables, and a provider
A workspace composes its own roles out of one app's keys
stages.ends: `custom_role` was applied, read by `permissionsFor` and written by nothing — a table, a resolver and a refusal rule with no way to reach any of them. `role.list`, `role.save` and `role.remove` are the three that make it real. `beyond_you` is the one to read twice: a workspace composing a role out of keys its author does not hold is the shortest path from “I can manage people” to “I can do anything” — make the role, assign it to yourself — and `saveRole` is the only writer that reaches the check. A role somebody still holds may not be deleted: the registry would stop carrying it, `permissionsFor` would resolve it to nothing, and they would keep their seat and be able to do nothing at all with no screen saying why.

stages.title: Agreements — versioned documents, an acceptance per person per version, and the wall until there is one
The vault is opened — consent, who looked, your data, and an erasure that shreds
The AI lane runs — a catalogue that syncs itself, one door out to every provider, a charge built on what the call really cost, and a nightly check against the bill we are sent
Notifications are filed — an event raised becomes a note in somebody's inbox
The daily sweep — erasure happens on a clock, and every run is recorded
A workspace's apps are turned on and off, and a workspace can move shard
Account security — sign out everywhere, and proving it is you again before something irreversible
A manifest changes while the deployment is up, and the composed surface forgets
A guard refuses a declared setting nothing names — the seam a handler reads one through is live; the completeness check over it is not
The kernel's remaining conveniences are each used by a lane or removed
A workspace runs its own retention ladder against its own customers, and ours freezes it
The deployment provisions itself — a product declares what it needs underneath it, and the reconciler makes it exist in the right jurisdiction, binds it, and reaps it after a drain
A workspace's records change shard, which is the only way its jurisdiction can — read-only while it copies, verified before it flips, and the source drained rather than emptied

A notification leaves the process — Web Push written out rather than depended on, a subscription filed under the door it was made at so it wears that workspace's own icon, and a keypair the console generates and never accepts
The documentation is two generated pages — what exists, derived from the engine; and how to add to it, which no generator can derive
An app ships a screen — a product's browser half is a chunk of its own, loaded when its workspace opens it, drawing that workspace's own records through the door it is handed
A workspace's brand reaches the screen — the surfaces it picked, and only the ones its products have
stages.ends: A workspace's brand reaches the two surfaces the deployment actually has, and only where the workspace asked for them. The editor stored the picks and NOTHING read them: the tile was painted from `mayBrand` alone — so a business that turned `app-icons` off still installed as itself — and no screen wore the theme at all. Being entitled to brand and asking to brand HERE are two questions, and reading only the first is what made every switch on that screen save and change nothing. `centre.view` now answers with the theme or with nothing, and `paintFor` reads the pick; the intersection is resolved where the surface is SERVED rather than where it is drawn, because every screen deciding for itself is how one product ends up branded and the next one beside it is not. On the page it is a second style element appended after the boot's — at equal specificity source order decides, and absent means EMPTY rather than untouched, or the last workspace's colours survive a switch.

stages.title: A screen asks the gate before it draws a control, rather than after it is pressed
stages.ends: `blockedBy` was declared in the kernel and called by nothing, so a control the gate would refuse was drawn, pressed, and failed — the refusal arriving as a toast over a form somebody had already filled in. The Ask is now built ONCE per request and asked twice: for this request's own gate, and for what else this caller could do. `centre.view` carries the second answer as `may`, only for what is BLOCKED (absent means allowed, which is also where a client that forgets the field lands), and every input is settled in memory by the locator so fifty operations cost fifty pure walks and no query. On the page it arrives through a CONTEXT rather than a prop — a prop is a thing every screen in every product has to remember to pass, and the one that forgets is not visibly different. An act names the OPERATION it calls rather than a verdict, so a screen never restates the gate's question in its own words; `Screen`'s primary and `Confirm`'s act both read it, and the words per gate are the design system's (`STOPPED`) rather than each screen's.

stages.title: Hello's remaining screens reach the workspace's own records — the report against its target, and writing a note
A one-off purchase — a credit pack, and becoming a business — through the same checkout
A plan is edited from the console, and everybody already on it keeps what they were sold
The wallet tops itself up — a standing instruction, a cooldown, and a decline the customer can read
Storage is metered rather than refused — the included amount is where the meter starts, and an empty wallet costs the writes and never the files
The deployment's legal identity is complete — the registered address it is written to, and whether selling where it sells needs a representative there
stages.ends: `IDENTITY.address` is the address on the licence rather than the Emirate, and either a representative is declared beside the sub-processors or a written decision says none is needed for where this deployment sells

stages.title: A stranger joins a workspace by themselves — a door the workspace opens, a role the app names, and a ceiling the plan sells (D23)
stages.ends: an app declares `access.joining`, composition refuses a joining role that is not a customer or that reads a tenant-scoped collection, `me.join` resolves its workspace from the door, and the customer ceiling refuses with a sentence naming the upgrade

stages.title: The interface speaks a second language — dictionaries, a language control, and the copy guard reading both
stages.ends: `Presentation.language` is offered on the Formats screen, every written string in `@engine/design` and `engine/one-space` resolves through a dictionary, and `tone.test.mjs` checks the voice in each language rather than only in English

stages.title: A collection says `searchable` and becomes findable — the write marks, a pass carries, erasure removes, and one filter is the boundary
stages.ends: `searchable` on a `CollectionSpec` produces the ledger, the `<collection>.search` operation, the quarter-hourly index pass and the removal on delete and on erasure, with `searching.test.mjs` making each of the four silences a test failure.

stages.title: The words arrive as they are written — one metered run, streamed, and the charge rides the last token
stages.ends: `ctx.stream` answers with an SSE `Response` from the same reserve, model and words `ctx.generate` uses; `generateStream` holds the same four bounds; a cancelled stream settles at the reserve and is corrected by the nightly check; `metering.test.mjs` asks the streaming lane every question it asks the other.

stages.title: A workspace asks to change its jurisdiction, and the ask is the only thing that is new
stages.ends: A workspace with `tenant:manage` can request a residency change from its own settings; the request is recorded and answered by an operator rather than granted, because Cloudflare fixes a database's jurisdiction at creation and the move is `op.tenant.move`'s `into` either way. `operator.test.mjs` sees the read behind the operator's queue of them, and nothing in the request path can begin a move by itself.

stages.title: A collection's `offline` policy reaches the browser — a write survives no signal, and a read answers without one
stages.ends: `offline` is read by the runtime and by the browser rather than only declared: `queue` holds a write until there is a connection and replays it once, `cache` answers a read from what was last seen and says how old it is, and `none` is honest about failing. `scripts/declared.test.mjs` fails on any field of a kernel declaration that no lane reads, which is the check that would have found this one.

stages.title: A collection narrows to part of a workspace — a location grant, and one filter the platform composes
stages.ends: `reach` on an `AppSpec` names the collection whose rows are the places and the field they nest by; `reachBy` on a collection names the field that says where one record is. A membership carries the places somebody works in, per app; a grant to a site covers everything under it, resolved at the read rather than frozen into the grant; and `null` — every membership until somebody is narrowed — is the whole workspace. The five generated verbs filter and refuse by themselves, `member.places` and `member.reach` are the roster's read and write, bounded by the granter's own reach, and `scripts/reach.test.mjs` fails on any statement over a narrowed table that neither carries the filter nor states why it is wide. The AUDIENCE of a notification is deliberately not narrowed — see `audienceFor`.

stages.title: A family takes a hue — one declared per product, never written at a call site
stages.ends: `tint` carries more than one hue, each declared once in `scene/tint.ts` as a constraint on the family, chosen by name rather than by value; `scene.test.mjs` still refuses a colour written into a screen; and two products wearing the family are visibly different and neither is nameable.

stages.title: Records move between workspaces — a garage becomes a business and its history goes with it
stages.ends: A workspace's records can be handed to another workspace the same account can already reach, with the ledger's provenance carried rather than restamped, refused where the destination's apps do not cover the source's collections, and audited on both sides. Until it exists the only path is an export and an import, which loses who did what and when.

stages.title: An operation's ceiling is in force — calls per minute, per caller, refused rather than declared
stages.ends: `OperationSpec.rate` is read inside `performOperation`, so both doors obey it and neither can forget; a caller past the ceiling is refused with a catalogued problem naming when to try again; and the counter is bounded rather than a row per call.

stages.title: A write says it worked — the sentence the operation declared, and the reads it made stale
stages.ends: `OperationSpec.outcome` reaches the browser and is applied by the one door: a successful write raises its declared message in its declared tone exactly once, and every operation it names in `invalidates` is re-read rather than left showing what was true before the press.

stages.title: OneInventory exists — the model, the one chokepoint that moves a balance, and the arithmetic under both
stages.ends: The manifest composes and the deployment prices every key it declares; `product`, `location`, `stock` and `ledger` are collections with the balance and the history opted out of every generated write; `stock.receive`, `stock.take` and `stock.adjust` go through one function that writes the event and the projection in one batch and refuses rather than clamping; and `ledger-chokepoint.test.mjs` fails on a second place that writes either table.

stages.title: A product's screens reach each other — the route is the app's, the prefix is the platform's
stages.ends: A mounted screen is handed `go`, which takes the app's OWN route; `routeIn` adds the workspace prefix for the nav and for a row inside a screen alike, so the two are one address rather than two copies of one expression. Until it existed an app's list could not open the record it listed, and the only way it could have was by writing the centre's address scheme into a product.

stages.title: A model can be shown something — the vision lane carries a picture, and the reserve counts it
stages.ends: `Ask.image` reaches the compat endpoint as a content part rather than being dropped, so `lane: "vision"` is a capability and not a name; `TOKENS_PER_IMAGE` puts the picture in the reserve, whether or not the units were counted by hand, because the settle cap makes an under-count permanently ours. And `ai-commits.test.mjs` fails on any operation that generates AND writes — a model fills anything, and a person commits.

stages.title: The release rail — a run ends, a person releases, and a late result may contradict neither
stages.ends: `process`, `process-item` and `job` are collections nothing writes by hand. Ending a run and releasing what it produced are separate acts under separate grants, because a green light is not a qualification. A quarantine freezes stock the chokepoint then REFUSES a take from, and lifts to needs-work — `release-ladder.test.mjs` fails on a release with no compare-and-set and on a lift that writes `released`. A late result that contradicts what is recorded is refused and names both facts; a late failure on a released run is a recall, which freezes what it can reach and NAMES what it cannot. And a job's trace is a query rather than a stored status, so a job correct on Tuesday acquires a concern on Thursday without anything about the job changing.

stages.title: A night’s work can tell somebody — a job raises events, and the nightly sweep uses it
stages.ends: `JobCtx` carries `tell` and `setting`, so a per-tenant job reaches the same inbox a request does — the same audience-by-permission, the same channel resolution, the same workspace numbers — and `eventsOf` counts a job’s `emits`, so a notification about something nobody was present for composes. The runner refuses an undeclared event and `refuseJob` refuses `emits` on a deployment-scope job, because a note is filed in a workspace. OneInventory’s expiry sweep is the first: it tells about CROSSINGS rather than states — `crossedOn` is arithmetic, so nothing is remembered, a repeat run names the same batches, and nobody is told the same thing every morning for a month. `job-tells.test.mjs` fails on a job that declares an event and never raises it.

stages.title: Labels — a QR from nothing, a printable sheet, and the decant label a hazard needs
stages.ends: `@engine/design` draws a QR itself (ISO/IEC 18004, byte mode, level M, versions 1–10) — hand-written, and only defensible because `qr.test.ts` DECODES what it produces with a reader that shares no code with it: unmasks, reads the format bits back, de-interleaves, checks every Reed-Solomon syndrome is zero, parses the payload. One symbology for everything we print, because two encoders are two ways for a tag to come out unscannable. `LabelSheet`/`Label`/`LabelText` are the one place in the system measured in millimetres, because a label has a physical size and a screen does not. OneInventory declares a GHS classification on a product and prints the decant label a decanted bottle legally needs — signal word, hazards, statements verbatim — says plainly that the diamond is not the regulated pictogram, and reports a classification that contradicts itself where the label is printed rather than refusing it. Printing a place or a product MINTS its code, and `label-once.test.mjs` fails on any statement that could re-issue one.

stages.title: Reports — what went, what was wrong, what to buy, and how much of it anybody wrote down
stages.ends: Every figure is derived from the ledger and nothing is stored, because a correction made in March changes what February consumed and a stored number never learns that. One operation answers all four, so a screen cannot show a month’s usage beside a fortnight’s losses. The HERO is the recorded share — the number that makes the product look bad, and the only one that says whether the others mean anything. Short and over stay apart, because netting them off draws a shelf that is wildly wrong as a shelf that is fine. What to buy is ordered by what runs out FIRST against the workspace’s own lead time, never by what is smallest — which is how a store room runs out of the thing that takes a month to get. `inferred-consumption.test.mjs` fails if the id a count mints and the prefix the report reads ever drift apart, or if a close stops naming its session.

stages.title: A screen can be gated on an entitlement, the way an operation already is
stages.ends: `ScreenSpec.features` names the capabilities a screen is FOR, and the boot read withholds the screen unless the plan includes one of them — so a destination the workspace did not buy has no nav row, no route and no way in by typing, which is the same three answers a flag already gave. It is asked on the SERVER rather than in the chrome: the page holds no plan, and giving it one would be a second round trip on the read every screen stands on plus a second opinion about what was bought. ANY rather than ALL, because a page carrying runs and work orders is worth opening on a tier that has only work orders. Composition refuses a screen gated on a key nothing sells, and deliberately does NOT count a screen as enforcement — hiding a nav row leaves the operations behind it callable, so a key whose only mention is a screen is still sold and withheld by nothing.

stages.title: A list narrows and pages — the generated read answers past the first fifty, and says how many there are
stages.ends: The generated `list` takes a filter over declared fields, a cursor and a count. `where` is equality over what the collection declares — a comparison language would be a query language arriving over the wire, and equality answers “this shelf's lines”, which is what a screen asks. The cursor is `(at, id)` rather than an offset, because rows arrive at the TOP: an offset of fifty on a collection that gained three since the first page steps over three the reader has never seen, silently. And the total is the collection's, counted over the same `WHERE` and WITHOUT the cursor, so it does not fall as somebody reads — a page of fifty out of two hundred was indistinguishable from a collection of fifty, and the screen drawing it said “fifty products” with complete confidence. The count runs BESIDE the page rather than before it, so the latency budget's `depth` is unchanged and only its trip count moved, 11 → 12, on purpose.

stages.title: Itemised things — one object for its whole life, and the kits composed of them
stages.ends: `unit` and `kit` are collections nothing can write by hand; issuing, taking back and retiring an object each move the shelf through the same chokepoint a box of gloves does, and `item-life.test.mjs` fails on a standing changed without one. A kit is checked against the recipe it was ASSEMBLED under, a build is refused while anything is short and a stray is reported rather than refused, and taking anything out of a built kit un-builds it. Our own label is the only code in a workspace that names one object rather than a type, which is what lets a count say "you have already counted that one".

stages.title: The guide and the milestones are ticked by what a workspace has actually done
stages.ends: A workspace's own tally — `tenant_event`, one row per (workspace, app, event), upserted on the way out of every successful operation that raises one — is what `guide.view` reads, so a step is ticked by what HAPPENED rather than by a screen deciding it looks done. Recorded beside `told` rather than inside it: the notification path returns early when an event has no audience, which is right for an inbox and wrong for a checklist. A milestone is said once and `tenant_milestone` is what stops it — `guide.seen` is a separate write, because a read that recorded the congratulation would spend it on a page somebody loaded and closed. And a step or milestone on an event only a JOB raises is refused at composition: the event exists, so the old check passed, and the step then sat unticked for ever because a sweep is not something anybody did.

stages.title: The spreadsheet somebody already has — the import, and the supplier it names
stages.ends: Nobody types in eight hundred products, so a paste of a stock list is the difference between a trial and a workspace. Quotes are parsed rather than stripped, the separator is read off the heading and a European decimal is not a thousands separator — each of those is a catalogue that looks complete and is wrong. The mapping is GUESSED and then SHOWN, editable, because a guess that puts the supplier's name in the product name for eight hundred rows is only catchable before it happens; every refused row comes back with its line number and its reason rather than being dropped. `one-planner.test.mjs` fails if the preview and the commit ever stop being one function — two walks of one sheet agree until the day they do not, and on that day nothing throws. A supplier is the last step of the reorder report's own workflow: it can say what to buy and, without this, not who to ring — and its own lead time beats the workspace's, which is the slowest supplier a place has.

stages.title: An operation's declared input is checked at the door, and `now` is one type
stages.ends: `checkAll` was reached by collection records and by settings and by nothing else, so every operation's `input` map was a declaration the tool catalogue, the OpenAPI document and every generated form were written from, with nothing standing behind it — a required field could be absent, a four-hundred-thousand-character bound was advisory, and a `day` could be any string. The symptom was never a 400: the field arrived as `undefined`, reached a statement, and D1 answered `Type 'undefined' not supported` in a 503 naming a value rather than a field. It is checked before the handler now, it names the field, and the generated verbs stay exempt because `records.ts` owns create-versus-update. `Ctx.now` is a STRING, the same as `JobCtx.now` — one word had two types in one framework and the one an app can write to a row is the string. And a job's budget is wall-clock from the start of the pass rather than from the logical instant, which had made every run handed a past instant break before the first workspace and report a clean night. `input-checked.test.mjs` holds the door; all of it was found by making real requests to a real worker, which nothing in this repository had done for an app.

stages.title: The other half of OneInventory, driven — and the quarantine that was a badge on a screen
stages.ends: Deliveries and the two expiry clocks, itemised objects and their life, kits and their recipes, the release ladder and the nightly sweep are all executed against a real database through the real door now, in `inventory-deep.test.ts`. It found the one that matters most: loading something into a run did not HOLD it. `freeze` set `standing = 'held'` on a failed or recalled run — the states where somebody has already noticed — and nothing held what was merely waiting to be signed for. So a tray whose cycle had ended and which no qualified person had released could be taken off the shelf and used on somebody, while the screen showed "waiting to be released". The gap between a machine finishing and a person signing for what came out of it is what this product has instead of deciding that a green light is a qualification, and until this stage the gap was a label. `process.put` holds; `process.release` stamps `ok`; `process.lift` unfreezes one item with a reason; receiving more of a held lot stays possible, because a quarantine is about what may LEAVE.

stages.title: The foot of a phone is a vignette, and everywhere an app declares is reachable from it
stages.ends: `--hem-bottom` was written by nobody, so the bottom vignette fell to its default of 1 on every screen: fully opaque, with the world's marks stopping dead at its top edge, which is a bar by the definition the top hem's own paragraphs give. Both hems ask the same question now — is anything actually behind this — and the easing is armed a frame after the first answer so a screen that arrives with nothing behind its nav is drawn that way rather than fading out of a hem it never should have had. And `nav: "secondary"` was drawn in the desktop rail and nowhere else, so an app declaring twelve destinations offered five to a phone and seven had no gesture at all. The bar's fifth slot is the way to the rest: a destination rather than a menu, wearing the app's mark, opening to say WHICH place somebody is in when they are inside one. `phoneNav` is the split as one function so the invariant — every declared destination in exactly one of the two lists — is something a test can ask about, and `design/test/reachable.test.tsx` asks it. D46.

stages.title: A raw ALTER is a 503 on every door, and every standard page wears the curtain
stages.ends: `stampOf` is a content hash over a module's statements, so ANY edit to a module replays ALL of them — and `ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN` is the one statement that cannot be replayed. Three modules carried one; the first edit to any of them threw `duplicate column name` out of `boot`, which is upstream of the router, so every door on the deployment answered 503 and the identity screen said "One could not start". It is invisible on a fresh database, therefore green in every suite, and it took the live deployment down. `columns` already existed for exactly this — it is reconciled against the live table rather than executed — so the three moved onto it and `refuseSql` now refuses the word ALTER outright, which makes the next one a test failure at the point of writing. The other half is what somebody SEES when a deployment cannot answer: `Opening` is the only screen that draws while One is starting, and there were three more — a stopped boot, a host that is not a workspace, a route that is not a screen — each its own layout, drifting. `Opening` takes a `stopped` and draws all four, so the ring completes instead of turning and the message replaces the rotating line, on the same gradient with the same grain. `Elsewhere.tsx` is deleted; `Sheet` went with it, because a centred panel is a `Group` in a `Center` and the third way of saying so had no renderer. D47.

stages.title: A person is a subject, and an operator may give them things
stages.ends: The console could see every workspace and nobody in one, and every way of handing something out began by knowing a workspace — so "give my friend a workspace at the top tier" was five acts across two screens with a human wait in the middle, and the decision behind it was recorded nowhere. `given` is that decision as an append-only row: an address, a plan × N workspaces or a number of credits, an optional term, a required reason, and the operator who signed it. It is made to an ADDRESS because a demo, a friend and a cash customer have usually never signed in; `upsertAccount` adopts what was written for them. A plan gift confers the right to found — counted WITH the bare commercial allowance, or an operator would have to raise a second number and forgetting refuses somebody the thing they were just given. `applyGifts` is the one application path and both doors call it: founding, and an operator applying to a workspace somebody already has. The plan and the allowance land in the same instant rather than on tomorrow's sweep; the gift's term travels onto the subscription so the nightly pass can end it, because bounding only the SPENDING would give a year of cash the tier for ever. And the workspace can tell: `money.view` carries `given`, so the shelf says "Given, and free until the first of December" where it printed a price over a card that does not exist. Two silent faults fell out — `topUp` and `grantAllowance` wrote a ledger line and an `UPDATE` that matched nothing on a workspace whose billing account was never opened, and one draft comped under the caller's app id while `renewAllowance` reads `MEMBERSHIP`, so the plan landed and the allowance was zero. Accounts and one account are console screens; no Stripe is in any of it. D48.

stages.title: A browser test does not gate a deploy
stages.ends: The CI job downloaded Chromium and its system libraries, then waited on twelve suites that render the shipped stylesheet and measure pixels — 97 seconds in the design package alone, 96 of them one file, more than every guard, typecheck and runtime suite put together. None of what they ask is what a deploy is waiting on: they answer whether a screen LOOKS right, and a deploy is asking whether the thing answers at all. They are `*.seen.test.*` now, excluded from every `test` config and run by `pnpm engine:seen`, which nothing in CI calls — so the cost is paid by whoever is changing a screen. Design's fast lane went 97s to 8s and the workflow installs no browser. The whole arrangement is a filename, which is why `scripts/seen.test.mjs` exists: it fails on a browser suite without the suffix, a suffixed suite that opens none, a package holding one with no `seen` script, a `test` config whose globs still pick one up — evaluated against the real filenames rather than read for the word `seen` — and a workflow that installs a browser again. `docs/guards.json` gained a `lane` field, because four registered guards are no longer reached by CI and a registry saying otherwise is worse than none. D49.

stages.title: Ambient motion is earned, and a field has a budget
stages.ends: The world's marks beat in SMIL inside a `<pattern>`, which is the only thing that repaints in one — and a repaint inside a paint server invalidates the whole fill, so every frame re-rasterised a tile and repainted a viewport-sized rect on the main thread, for as long as a screen was open, competing with scrolling. Measured at the density a list screen asks for: the fine lattice was 2,820 placements, 394 live animations and 504 KB of markup; the line-art family 432 and 10. `motionFor` is the one decision now, from a stored choice and what the device says about itself, and it answers in two tiers — ESSENTIAL motion (arrival, travel, a press, a chart drawing: short, one-shot, composited, and carrying meaning) is assumed, AMBIENT motion (endless, full-screen, never composited) is EARNED. A fine pointer is the entry condition because a mid-range phone reports eight cores and cannot report a mouse; memory and cores only veto, and their silence is not a refusal. `useStillness` became a projection of it rather than a second answer. The other half is the cost that a motion setting cannot reach: a still field is still a string to parse and a tree to rasterise, so `MARKS` caps what a field may emit and the TILE shrinks rather than the cell — the same picture repeating sooner, against half a megabyte on every screen. Measured after: 588 placements, 133 KB, and no live animations on the default path. And the switch is reachable at last: every keyframe answered `data-reduce-motion` and nothing set it, `applyAppearance` read a value nothing wrote — `Look and motion` is both, on the device rather than the account, and it says which fact about the hardware decided. D50.

stages.title: A workspace is founded with the products somebody chose
stages.ends: `me.tenant.create` founded with `apps: [deps.appId]` and `deps.appId` was the string `"hello"`, hardcoded in the worker — so every workspace anybody made held the reference app whatever they came for, and the only way to change it afterwards was to ask an operator to do it in the console. A deployment that serves several products and can only hand out the first is one product with the others built. Founding takes the ids now, narrowed to a `sells` catalogue that is deliberately a separate list from what is SERVED — a product mid-build stays mounted for the workspaces an operator put it in and comes out of one line — and refuses an empty choice, because a workspace with no product is a name and an address with nothing to open. `me.products` reads the manifests so the wizard cannot hold a second catalogue that goes stale, and `app.list`/`app.add`/`app.remove` let an owner change it later, with the last one un-removable: a workspace with nothing on cannot reach the screen that would switch something back on. Switching one on is a row and nothing else, because every product's schema is applied to every shard at boot. The first name for those three was `product.*`, which SILENTLY REPLACED OneInventory's own `product.list` — platform operations are merged over an app's generated CRUD on purpose — so `compose` refuses a shadowing id outright now instead of resolving it. D51.
